IP addresses contain a user’s legal identity.
IP addresses prove intent.
IP addresses are passwords.
quiz.answer: Network addressing can be shared, translated, proxied, or dynamically assigned.
quiz.explanation: Network identity and human identity are distinct evidence questions.

summary: Network records are strongest when correlated with endpoint and identity sources.
Encrypted traffic may hide content while leaving some metadata visible.

lessons.title: Correlating Memory, Endpoint, and Network Evidence
lessons.description: Build a corroborated finding from multiple evidence types and explicitly identify what remains unknown.
learningObjectives: align process, command-line, network, and time evidence
identify a suspicious sequence without calling it malicious prematurely
specify the next validating evidence

notes.text: Correlation example

Suppose a memory image contains a process whose command line references a network client, endpoint telemetry records a connection from the same process around the same time, and DNS telemetry resolves the associated hostname shortly beforehand. Together these records support a stronger sequence than any one source alone, but they still do not by themselves establish intent.

items: Preserve each source’s timestamp and semantics.
Check process ancestry and executable path.
Compare network destination, timing, and relevant endpoint identity/session records.
State what would falsify the working hypothesis.

quiz.question: What is the primary analytical benefit of correlating memory and network evidence?
options: Independent sources can support or challenge the same activity sequence.
Correlation makes every artifact automatically true.
Correlation removes clock skew.
Correlation proves user intent.
quiz.answer: Independent sources can support or challenge the same activity sequence.
quiz.explanation: Correlation increases confidence by combining artifacts with different limitations.

summary: Cross-domain correlation is a core forensic reasoning skill.
Good findings preserve uncertainty rather than turning a suspicious sequence into an unsupported verdict.

tasks.title: Assess a Synthetic Memory-and-Network Finding
tasks.description: Evaluate a synthetic Volatility-style process tree plus endpoint and network evidence.
tasks.problemStatement: A process has an unusual parent, a command-line argument referencing a remote resource, and a network connection at a matching time. Write a finding that distinguishes evidence, inference, and required corroboration.
objectives: test at least one benign alternative
tasks.hint: Use “supports escalation for further examination” rather than declaring compromise solely from the listed artifacts.
tasks.solutionCode:
Observation: the process tree shows an unusual parent/child relationship and the command line contains a remote resource. Endpoint and network records show activity in the same time window.
Assessment: the evidence supports escalation for deeper examination.
Alternative explanation: a legitimate administrative tool or application helper process may have generated the sequence.
Next tests: verify executable path/hash/signer, persistence context, user/session identity, and independent network records.
tasks.solutionExplanation: This is the correct forensic posture for triage: identify a high-value lead, preserve uncertainty, and specify discriminating evidence.

modules.title: Timelines, Validation, Reporting, and Final Project
modules.description: Turn artifacts into defensible findings through timeline construction, tool validation, hypothesis testing, professional reporting, and a complete controlled case reconstruction project.

lessons.title: Forensic Timeline Construction
lessons.description: Create timelines that preserve source provenance and timestamp meaning rather than hiding uncertainty behind a single date column.
learningObjectives: design a source-preserving timeline schema
normalize timestamps with documented assumptions
identify gaps and contradictions

notes.text: A timeline is a derived model
source | source_time | normalized_time | artifact | event | subject | confidence | limitation

items: Keep original evidence timestamps intact and derive normalized values separately.
Use event semantics that match the artifact.
Record time zone/offset and clock assumptions.
Mark gaps and contradictions rather than inventing continuity.

quiz.question: What makes a forensic timeline reproducible?
options: Each event is traceable to a source artifact and the timestamp semantics are documented.
All timestamps are converted without recording the source.
Only one artifact source is used.
Uncertainty is removed from the final table.
quiz.answer: Each event is traceable to a source artifact and the timestamp semantics are documented.
quiz.explanation: A timeline is derived analysis and must retain provenance and assumptions.

summary: Timelines organize evidence; they do not replace the underlying artifacts.
Source-preserving design makes later review possible.

lessons.title: Tool Validation and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Learn how to test forensic tools and document the conditions under which results are trustworthy.
learningObjectives: define a tool-validation question
use known test data and expected results
record versions, configuration, and limitations

notes.text: Validation is bounded

NIST’s Computer Forensics Tool Testing program and SWGDE guidance emphasize testing forensic tools against defined functions. A validation activity should specify the capability being tested, controlled input, expected result, actual result, and environment.

items: Use known test datasets that contain artifacts with known characteristics.
Record tool version, operating environment, relevant settings, and test procedure.
Where feasible, compare results against an independent method or trusted reference.
Retain test evidence so the conclusion about the tool can be revisited.

notes.text: Being widely used does not by itself validate a forensic tool for the function you rely upon.

quiz.question: What is the strongest example of a forensic-tool validation activity?
options: Testing a defined function with known input and expected output.
Using the newest version without testing it.
Choosing a tool because it is popular.
Running a tool once and assuming all plugins are validated.
quiz.answer: Testing a defined function with known input and expected output.
quiz.explanation: Validation is empirical and function-specific.

summary: Tool validation should be tied to the actual capability used in an examination.
Version and configuration belong in the reproducibility record.

lessons.title: Hypothesis Testing and Investigative Reasoning
lessons.description: Use competing explanations to reduce confirmation bias and focus collection on discriminating evidence.
learningObjectives: write competing hypotheses
identify evidence that would distinguish them
document unresolved questions

notes.text: Observation is not a verdict

Suppose a document timestamp changes at 21:10Z. Possible explanations include an interactive edit, an automated job, a synchronization client, or another system process. The examiner should identify evidence that distinguishes these explanations rather than selecting the most interesting story first.

items: Form at least two plausible explanations for an important observation.
Identify what evidence should exist under each explanation.
Search for evidence that could falsify the preferred hypothesis.
Record what remains unresolved.

quiz.question: Why use competing hypotheses in forensic analysis?
options: To seek evidence that can distinguish or falsify alternative explanations.
To avoid reaching any conclusion.
To replace technical evidence with opinion.
To reduce the amount of documentation.
quiz.answer: To seek evidence that can distinguish or falsify alternative explanations.
quiz.explanation: Competing hypotheses help reduce confirmation bias and make analysis testable.

summary: Good forensic reasoning is explicitly falsifiable where practical.
A limitation is a result, not a failure: it identifies what the evidence cannot answer.

lessons.title: Forensic Reporting and Expert Communication
lessons.description: Write findings that are traceable to evidence and that clearly distinguish observations, inferences, limitations, and conclusions.
learningObjectives: structure a forensic report
write evidence-grounded findings
state limitations precisely

notes.text: Report components

items: Scope and authority
Evidence inventory and integrity information
Methods and tools/versions
Findings with evidence references
Analysis and correlation
Limitations and uncertainty
Conclusions answering the defined questions

notes.text: A strong finding typically has the form: Observation → Corroboration → Interpretation → Limitation. This prevents a derived interpretation from being mistaken for a direct artifact observation.
Use language proportional to evidence. “The artifact records…” is often more defensible than “the user did…” when attribution is incomplete.

quiz.question: Which practice best supports independent review of a forensic finding?
options: Reference the evidence source, method, and limitation for the finding.
Provide only a narrative conclusion.
Omit tool versions.
Treat derived interpretations as direct observations.
quiz.answer: Reference the evidence source, method, and limitation for the finding.
quiz.explanation: Traceability lets another reviewer understand and test the reasoning.

summary: Professional reporting is part of forensic method, not an afterthought.
Clear limitations improve rather than weaken technical credibility.

lessons.title: Case Closure, Archiving, and Reproducibility
lessons.description: Prepare a case for future review by preserving evidence, derived outputs, notes, and validation material.
learningObjectives: define a minimum reproducibility package
explain archive integrity and access controls
prepare a closure checklist

notes.text: Closure checklist

items: Evidence inventory and custody complete.
Acquisition hashes and verification records retained.
Working-copy provenance documented.
Scripts, tool versions, configurations, queries, and search terms retained.
Final report and exhibits are linked to evidence identifiers.
Archive location, access controls, and retention requirements documented.

notes.text: SWGDE archiving guidance treats long-term retention as part of the forensic process because evidence and analytical results can be needed well after the initial examination.

quiz.question: Why should case-analysis scripts be retained?
options: They may be needed to reproduce derived outputs and understand transformations.
Scripts are unrelated to reproducibility.
Retaining scripts changes the evidence.
Scripts replace custody documentation.
quiz.answer: They may be needed to reproduce derived outputs and understand transformations.
quiz.explanation: Derived artifacts should be explainable from preserved methods and code.

summary: Case closure includes the information needed for future review.
Archive controls should preserve integrity and controlled access.

project.name: Forensic Case Reconstruction Workbench
project.description: Build a read-only Python workbench for a controlled forensic evidence directory. The workbench inventories files, computes SHA-256 hashes, records filesystem metadata exposed by Python, identifies duplicate content, and produces structured outputs for subsequent forensic analysis. The final assessment combines evidence integrity, filesystem context, automation, reproducibility, reporting, and cautious interpretation without pretending to replace validated forensic acquisition or full forensic suites.
steps: Create a synthetic evidence directory with nested files and at least one pair of identical files under different names.
Treat the directory as a verified working copy from an authorized acquisition or export; record the evidence identifier outside the evidence tree.
Create `forensic_core.py` and `main.py` from the complete code below.
Run the program with Python 3 using `python main.py <evidence_dir> --output <report_dir>`.
Confirm that the report directory is outside the evidence directory and that the program refuses an output path located inside the evidence tree.
Compare the reported regular-file count to an independent file count.
Inspect `file_inventory.csv` and `file_inventory.json` and verify path, size, SHA-256, and timestamp fields.
Inspect `duplicate_groups.json` and verify the deliberately duplicated files share the same content digest.
Run the program twice without changing evidence and confirm unchanged files retain the same SHA-256 values.
In a separate working-copy experiment, modify one file and verify that its content digest changes; do not perform this test on preserved original evidence.
Write a findings note that separates measured observations from derived duplicate groups and interpretation.
Retain the project code, test inputs, generated outputs, hashes, Python version, and validation observations as a reproducibility package.

code.main.py:
from __future__ import annotations

import argparse
import sys
from pathlib import Path
from forensic_core import collect_files, write_csv, write_duplicates, write_json

def parse_args() -> argparse.Namespace:
    parser = argparse.ArgumentParser(description='Read-only forensic triage of an authorized evidence directory.')
    parser.add_argument('evidence_dir', type=Path, help='Authorized working copy or evidence export.')
    parser.add_argument('--output', type=Path, default=Path('forensic_report'), help='Separate report directory.')
    return parser.parse_args()

def main() -> int:
    args = parse_args()
    evidence_dir = args.evidence_dir.resolve()
    output = args.output.resolve()
    if not evidence_dir.is_dir():
        print(f'Evidence directory does not exist: {evidence_dir}', file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    if output == evidence_dir or evidence_dir in output.parents:
        print('Refusing to write reports inside the evidence directory.', file=sys.stderr)
        return 2
    output.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)
    records = collect_files(evidence_dir)
    write_csv(records, output / 'file_inventory.csv')
    write_json(records, output / 'file_inventory.json')
    write_duplicates(records, output / 'duplicate_groups.json')
    print(f'Files examined: {len(records)}')
    print(f'Reports written to: {output}')
    print('Evidence directory was read only by this application.')
    return 0

if __name__ == '__main__':
    raise SystemExit(main())

project.explanation: The workbench has a deliberate separation of concerns. `main.py` validates the evidence/output boundary, creates the reporting directory, and coordinates processing. `forensic_core.py` performs deterministic file enumeration, SHA-256 hashing, timestamp conversion to UTC ISO format, JSON/CSV serialization, and duplicate grouping. The tool never writes inside the evidence directory and therefore demonstrates a basic read-only analytical boundary. The final project also requires independent counting, repeat-run comparison, a controlled mutation experiment on a non-original working copy, and a written findings note. Those checks connect automation to forensic method: generated data remains derived evidence, and the examiner still has to interpret semantics, corroborate important findings, preserve limitations, and maintain reproducibility.
validationPlan: Test an empty evidence directory and verify that the inventory reports zero regular files.
Test nested directories and filenames containing spaces.
Test a zero-byte file and verify it receives the SHA-256 digest for an empty byte stream.
Create two identical files under different paths and verify one duplicate hash group contains both.
Modify one working-copy file and verify only its changed digest differs.
Attempt to place the report directory inside the evidence root and confirm the program refuses it.
Run the tool twice on unchanged evidence and compare the inventory hashes and file count.
Inspect the source to confirm that evidence paths are only read and never opened for writing.
limitations: Python filesystem timestamps are operating-system-dependent and are not a substitute for filesystem-native forensic parsing.
The project does not acquire evidence or create forensic disk images.
The project does not recover deleted data or parse raw unallocated space.
The project does not parse registry, memory, mobile, cloud-provider, or browser-specific formats.
A matching SHA-256 digest establishes matching observed bytes to the properties and limitations of the hash function; it does not establish authorship or provenance.
Legal, organizational, privacy, retention, and evidentiary requirements remain case-specific and are outside this educational implementation.
